You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 0.76 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal (weak); Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 6800 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weakest excitation; Ip = 8 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 10 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       0.56   0.566    11.6       -    0.0314  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S2      0.558   0.563    11.2       -    0.0457  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       2.24    2.26    35.4   0.329     0.228  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S4      0.334   0.339    8.95       -   0.00508  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S5      0.573   0.581    15.7       -    0.0329  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S6      0.459   0.462     6.1       -    0.0211  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor-node $R_L$ from a piezo energy harvester.
    *   $V_{out}$ range: $1.8\text{V}$ to $3.6\text{V}$.
    *   Ripple $\le 0.05\text{V}$.
    *   Startup $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$.
    *   Settling $dv \le 0.02\text{V}$.
    *   Piezo: $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ ($25\text{nF}$) and $20\text{M}\Omega$.
    *   Open-circuit voltage amplitude: $V_{oc} \approx 0.76\text{V}$.

    *   `sshi_fbr`: This is a hybrid of SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) and a Full-Bridge Rectifier.
        *   Connectivity: FBR (4x DSCH) + an L-S branch in parallel with the piezo.
        *   Results: Passes S3 (strong excitation), but fails S1, S2, S4, S5, S6.
        *   Crucially, the output doesn't reach $1.8\text{V}$ for S4, S5, S6.
        *   $t_{up}$ is too slow.
        *   Ripple is too high (this is likely because $C_{out}$ is too small or the energy delivered per cycle is too low/bursty).
        *   Settling is poor (too slow time constant).
    *   `sece_inductive` and `sshi_half_bridge`: Failed screening.

    *   $V_{oc} \approx 0.76\text{V}$ is very low. Standard FBR loses $2 \times 0.25\text{V} = 0.5\text{V}$, leaving only $0.26\text{V}$, which can't reach $1.8\text{V}$ without a boost mechanism.
    *   SSHI is designed to flip the voltage across $C_p$, effectively multiplying the voltage.
    *   The `sshi_fbr` used a full bridge *after* the L-S flip. However, the FBR diodes still create a significant drop.
    *   The failure on S4, S5, S6 indicates insufficient power. S4 is the weakest excitation ($I_p = 8\mu\text{A}$).
    *   The ripple and settling issues suggest the energy delivered in pulses is not being smoothed correctly, or the pulses are too far apart relative to the load.

    *   To get $1.8\text{V}$ from a $0.76\text{V}$ source, we need a voltage boost.
    *   SSHI is a great way to increase the voltage across $C_p$. The peak voltage becomes $V_{pk} \approx \frac{4 V_{oc}}{1 + \frac{R_{load}}{R_{piezo}}}$? No, it's more like $V_{pk}$ increases as $\tan(\phi)$ where $\phi$ is related to $t_{on}$.
    *   Wait, the SSHI basic principle: The inductor $L$ flips the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks.
    *   A standard SSHI circuit typically uses a switch and an inductor to flip $V_{Cp}$, then rectifies.
    *   The problem with `sshi_fbr` was perhaps the diode drops. Can we use synchronous rectification?
    *   Synchronous rectification using switches (S) instead of diodes (D) would eliminate the $0.25\text{V}-0.5\text{V}$ drop.

    *   We need to flip the voltage across $C_p$ and then transfer the charge to $C_{out}$.
    *   Standard SSHI: $L$ flips $V_{Cp}$ at the peaks.
    *   To transfer charge to $V_{out}$:
        *   At the positive peak of $V_{Cp}$, use a switch/diode to move charge to $V_{out}$.
        *   At the negative peak of $V_{Cp}$, use a switch/diode to move charge to $V_{out}$.
    *   But to *boost* the voltage, we must flip $V_{Cp}$ *before* charging $V_{out}$.
    *   Actually, the "classic" SSHI involves flipping $V_{Cp}$ to avoid the $C_p$ opposing the current source.
    *   Let's try a Synchronous SSHI (S-SSHI) or a similar topology that uses synchronous switches for rectification.

    *   Current source $I_p$ charges $C_p$.
    *   When $V_{Cp}$ reaches a peak, $L$ is connected in parallel to flip $V_{Cp}$.
    *   Then, the current continues to charge $C_p$ in the new direction.
    *   To extract energy:
        *   Positive half: $V_{Cp} > V_{out}$? (Hard, since $V_{oc}$ is low).
        *   We need the voltage to build up on $C_p$ first.
        *   If we use a switch to connect $C_p$ to $C_{out}$ only when $V_{Cp}$ is very high.

    *   The `sshi_fbr` failed mainly on power. Let's try a simpler but more efficient SSHI.
    *   Standard SSHI structure:
        1.  Piezo $C_p$ in parallel with a rectifier.
        2.  An inductor $L$ and a switch $S_{flip}$ that closes at peaks.
    *   The rectifier can be a full-bridge of diodes (FBR) or synchronous.
    *   Wait, if the output needs to be $1.8\text{V}$, and $V_{oc}$ is $0.76\text{V}$, we *must* use the inductor to boost the voltage.
    *   The "flip" happens: $V_{Cp}$ goes from $V_{peak}$ to $-V_{peak}$.
    *   Then the current source $I_p$ charges it from $-V_{peak}$ up to $V_{peak}$.
    *   The total voltage swing is $2 V_{peak}$.
    *   If we rectify this, we can reach higher voltages.

    *   Let's try a topology where the inductor is used to boost the voltage into the storage capacitor.
    *   A "Boost-Rectifier" or a "Synchronous SSHI".
    *   Let's try a topology:
        -   Inductor $L$ in series with the piezo.
        -   Switch $S_1$ to ground to build energy in $L$.
        -   Diode $D_1$ to $V_{out}$ to transfer energy.
        -   This is a basic boost converter. But we have an AC source.

    *   Let's try a modified SSHI:
        -   Piezo ($pzp, pzn$)
        -   $L$ between $pzp$ and $n1$.
        -   Switch $S_1$ between $n1$ and $pzn$ (the "flip" switch).
        -   Rectification:
            -   $D_1$ from $pzp$ to $out$.
            -   $D_2$ from $pzn$ to $out$.
            -   $D_3$ from $0$ to $pzp$.
            -   $D_4$ from $0$ to $pzn$.
            -   (This is the `sshi_fbr` again).

    *   Why did `sshi_fbr` fail?
        -   The energy delivered per cycle was too low for S4, S5, S6.
        -   $V_{oc} = 0.76\text{V}$.
        -   The FBR has a $0.5\text{V}$ drop.
        -   If the SSHI flip boosts $V_{Cp}$ to, say, $2\text{V}$, then $2\text{V} - 0.5\text{V} = 1.5\text{V}$, which is still below $1.8\text{V}$.
        -   We need to reduce the diode drop.

    *   What if we use a half-bridge rectifier (one diode) but only charge on one half-cycle?
        -   No, that loses half the energy.
    *   What if we use a synchronous rectifier?
        -   S1: $pzp$ to $out$ (closes when $V_{pzp} > V_{out}$)
        -   S2: $pzn$ to $out$ (closes when $V_{pzn} > V_{out}$)
        -   This requires more SYNC controllers. We have 2.

    *   Let's try a "Parallel-SSHI" (P-SSHI) with a better rectifier.
    *   Wait, there's a known topology called "SECE" (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction).
    *   SECE:
        -   Inductor $L$ is used to extract charge from $C_p$ at the peaks.
        -   $L$ is connected to $pzp$ and $pzn$ through switches.
        -   $L$ then transfers the energy to $C_{out}$.
    *   Let's refine the SECE:
        -   $S_1$ connects $pzp \to L$.
        -   $S_2$ connects $pzn \to L$.
        -   $L$ is connected to $out$ via a diode $D_1$.
        -   At the positive peak of $V_{pzp}$, $S_1$ closes, $L$ charges.
        -   At the negative peak of $V_{pzp}$, $S_2$ closes, $L$ charges.
        -   $D_1$ allows $L$ to dump energy into $C_{out}$.
        -   (This is similar to the `sece_inductive` that failed). Why did it fail?
        -   `sece_inductive` had: $S_1$ ($pzp, n1$), $S_2$ ($pzn, n1$), $L_1$ ($n1, n2$), $D_1$ ($n2, out$).
        -   $G_1$ (pos peak), $G_2$ (neg peak).
        -   This is a correct SECE. Maybe the $L$ value was wrong? But the screening failed.
        -   Screening failure usually means the topology is fundamentally incapable of delivering the power.

    *   Let's reconsider the `sshi_fbr`. It *did* pass the screening. It just didn't deliver *enough* power to meet the $1.8\text{V}$ target on all conditions.
    *   If the FBR is the problem, how to replace it?
    *   What if we use a charge pump? No, too complex.
    *   What if we use a simpler rectifier?
    *   A half-bridge rectifier: $D_1$ from $pzp$ to $out$, $D_2$ from $pzn$ to $out$, and a capacitor $C_{bias}$ from $pzn$ to $0$.
    *   Wait, the most efficient way to get rid of diode drops is synchronous rectification.
    *   But we only have 2 SYNC controllers.
    *   We can use one SYNC to flip $V_{Cp}$ and one SYNC to... what?
    *   Actually, let's look at the SSHI flip again. The inductor $L$ is in parallel with $C_p$ during the flip.
    *   If we use the inductor to *boost* the voltage, the inductor should be in series with the path to $V_{out}$.

    *   Let's try the "SSHI with a Capacitor-based DC-DC" or a simpler "Inductive-Boost SSHI".
    *   How about this:
        -   S1: $pzp$ to $n1$ (ctrl G1)
        -   L1: $n1$ to $out$
        -   D1: $pzp$ to $out$
        -   D2: $pzn$ to $out$
        -   D3: $0$ to $pzp$
        -   D4: $0$ to $pzn$
        -   This is just a weird FBR.

    *   Let's go back to basics. We need $1.8\text{V}$. $V_{oc}$ is $0.76\text{V}$.
    *   An SSHI circuit can boost the voltage across $C_p$ to $V_{peak}$.
    *   $V_{peak} = \frac{V_{oc}}{1 - \text{something}}$.
    *   If $V_{peak}$ reaches $2.5\text{V}$, a Schottky diode ($0.25\text{V}$) will let it pass to $V_{out} = 2.25\text{V}$.
    *   So the `sshi_fbr` was almost there. Why did it fail S4, S5, S6?
    *   S4: $I_p = 8\mu\text{A}$ (weakest).
    *   S5: $f = 80\text{Hz}$ (low frequency).
    *   S6: $C_p = 30\text{nF}$ (higher capacitance, harder to flip).
